nodes.question: What is a major challenge in managing NIS in the archipelago?
nodes.answer: A major challenge is the lack of practical tools to assess risks, which hampers the implementation of management policies and strategies.
nodes.paragraph: 2018; Ferrario et al. 2020; Castro et al. 2019; 2021a; 2021b, 2022). Maritime traffic also has a key role in the local dispersion of NIS (Parretti et al. 2020; Cas- tro et al. 2022a). However, the risk posed by this local dispersal mechanism remains poorly studied. This is particularly worrisome due to the recent detection of potentially invasive NIS such as the brown seaweed Rugulopteryx okamurae (Bernal-lb ez et al. 2022) and the crab Cronius ruber (Sch fer et al. 2019). Despite global, regional and local concerns, NIS management policies and strategies to control and surveil the local proliferation of NIS in the archi- pelago remain scarce (e.g., Castro et al. 2024). The lack of control mechanisms to avoid the local spread and proliferation of NIS is partly related to the lack of practical, meaningful tools to assess risks across the region, which can be particularly problematic to marine conservation efforts such as creating and implementing Marine Protected Areas and Marine Reserves. nodes.question: What environmental vulnerabilities does the Philippines face due to its location within the Ring of Fire?
nodes.answer: The Philippines is particularly vulnerable to seismic and climatological disturbances, experiencing issues such as changing weather patterns and increased incidences of drought and flooding.
nodes.paragraph: Located within the Ring of Fire along the Western Pacific, the Philippines is particularly vulnerable to seismic and climatological disturbances (Pulhin & Tapia, 2021; Tolentino et al., 2016). CC-induced warming is expected to aggravate unpredictable weather patterns that could potentially result in drier dry months and wetter wet months in the Philippines. Inland riverine biodiversity, integral to the subsistence livelihood of many vulnerable rural communities in the country, will be harshly affected by changing water levels and increas- ing incidences of drought and flooding (Tolentino et al., 2016). As many riparian vegeta- tions are non-resilient to drought effects (see Jha et al. (2019a), such perturbations further hinder riverine ecological functioning (Jha et al. (2019b) because the two systems are inex- tricably connected (Hoppenreijs et al., 2022). Indeed, the current freshwater biodiversity in the Philippines is already severely declining, with many freshwater bodies in poor condi- tions (Magbanua et al., 2017; Papa & Briones, 2017; van der Ploeg et al., 2017). Approxi- mately 40 (Pineda-Ofreneo, 2019) and 180 (Bengwayan, 2019) of the 421 principal rivers in the country are considered biologically dead or severely polluted, respectively.

nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Climate action|Sea level rise|Impact on low-lying islands_qna_004
nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What existential threat do the counties face if no adaptation measures are implemented regarding sea level rise?
nodes.answer: The continued sea level rise poses an existential threat to the region.
nodes.paragraph: These three counties provide an ideal and compelling case study given the frequent flood - ing from Hurricanes and tropical storms (e.g., Hurricane Andrew in 1992 and Hurricane Irma in 2017), the large population at low elevations, increasing threats from SLR, and the growing need for climate adaptation measures for infrastructure. Coastal areas in the study region are especially vulnerable to SLR as it is projected that the sea level will rise about 6 to 10 inches by 2030 and 14 to 26 inches by 2060. In the long term, SLR is projected to be 31 to 61 inches by 2100 (Sea Level Rise Work Group 2015 ). Considering that the average elevation of Broward County, Miami-Dade County, and Palm Beach County is 72, 72, and 84 inches, respectively, the continued SLR will pose an existential threat to the region if no adaptation measures are to be implemented. 1 See the 2020 Census data for Broward County ( https://data.census.gov/all? q =Broward%20County,%20 Florida ), Miami-Dade County ( https://data.census.gov/all? q =Miami-Dade%20County,%20Florida ), and Palm Beach County ( https://data.census.gov/all?
